activity.overview: Practice taking notes in your own words and recording where each fact came from.
activity.passage:
How researchers take notes

Researchers do not copy whole sentences. They read a part of the text, look away, and write the important idea in their own words, using only a few key words. Then they write down where the idea came from, so they can find it again and give credit.

Read this paragraph from a book called Tiny Flyers:

"The ruby-throated hummingbird is one of the smallest birds in North America. It weighs about as much as a penny. To stay in the air, it beats its wings more than 50 times every second, which makes the humming sound that gives the bird its name. All that flapping uses a great deal of energy, so a hummingbird must drink nectar from hundreds of flowers every day."

Here is one researcher's note: "wings beat 50+ times a second = humming sound (Tiny Flyers)".

questions.prompt: Why do researchers write notes in their own words instead of copying sentences?
Write a note, using only key words, about how much a ruby-throated hummingbird weighs.
Write a note about why hummingbirds must drink nectar from hundreds of flowers. Use your own words.
Look at the researcher's note. Why does it end with (Tiny Flyers)?
Write one focus question you could research next about hummingbirds.
